# Use case 5: cell-cell communication networks

Cell-cell communication (CCC) is commonly inferred from scRNA-seq data
based on the expression of ligands in sender cell types and their receptors
in receiver cell types. The result is naturally represented as a directed
graph of cell types. Here, we will use __GraphExperiment__ to store CCC
networks in the `colGraphs` slot of an object containing pseudobulk
expression profiles (i.e., with cell types in columns). This use case
demonstrates that observation-level graphs can be stored at any
resolution, including cells (see use case 4), cell types,
samples, or species (see use cases 6 and 7).

We will infer CCC with __LIANA__ [@dimitrov2022comparison], a framework
that runs multiple CCC inference methods and combines their results into a
consensus ranking of ligand-receptor interactions. We chose LIANA because
a systematic comparison of CCC methods showed that no single method
consistently outperformed the others, and that the choice of method
strongly affects predictions [@dimitrov2022comparison], making a consensus
approach a sensible default. Other tools, such as NicheNet
[@browaeys2020nichenet], address a complementary question (i.e., which
ligands best explain gene expression changes in receiver cells), and
their output (ligand-target gene links) could be stored in `rowGraphs`.
We will use scRNA-seq data of human pancreatic islets
from @baron2016single, available in the __scRNAseq__
package [@risso2025scrnaseq].

```{r here}
#| message: false
#| eval: true

library(here)
library(GraphExperiment)
library(scRNAseq)
library(scuttle)
library(liana)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggraph)

set.seed(123) # for reproducibility
```

## Data description and processing

We will first load the data and, to keep this example lightweight,
randomly sample up to 100 cells per cell type, keeping only
cell types with at least 20 cells.

```{r}
# Load data
sce <- BaronPancreasData("human")
sce

# Check annotated cell types
table(sce$label)

# Sample up to 100 cells per cell type
idx <- split(seq_len(ncol(sce)), sce$label)
idx <- unlist(lapply(idx, function(i) if(length(i) > 100) sample(i, 100) else i))
sce <- sce[, sort(idx)]

# Keep only cell types with at least 20 cells
sce <- sce[, sce$label %in% names(which(table(sce$label) >= 20))]
table(sce$label)

# Normalize data
sce <- logNormCounts(sce)

sce
```

## Inferring cell-cell communication

To reduce memory usage, we will only keep genes encoding ligands and
receptors in LIANA's consensus resource. Then, we will infer CCC
with four methods (NATMI, Connectome, log2FC, and SingleCellSignalR), and
aggregate their results into a consensus ranking.

```{r}
# Keep only genes in the ligand-receptor resource
lr_resource <- select_resource("Consensus")[["Consensus"]]
lr_genes <- unique(unlist(strsplit(
    c(lr_resource$source_genesymbol, lr_resource$target_genesymbol), "_"
)))
sce_lr <- sce[rownames(sce) %in% lr_genes, ]

# Infer CCC with multiple methods and aggregate results
liana_res <- liana_wrap(
    sce_lr, idents_col = "label", resource = "Consensus",
    method = c("natmi", "connectome", "logfc", "sca"), verbose = FALSE
)
liana_agg <- liana_aggregate(liana_res, verbose = FALSE)

head(liana_agg)
```

We will keep interactions with aggregate rank < 0.01 and
create a directed graph of cell types in which edges point from
sender to receiver cell types, edge weights represent the number of
interactions, and edge attributes include the ligand-receptor pairs.
Self-loops represent autocrine signaling.

```{r}
# Filter interactions and summarize by sender/receiver pairs
ccc_edges <- liana_agg |>
    filter(aggregate_rank < 0.01) |>
    mutate(lr_pair = paste0(ligand.complex, "->", receptor.complex)) |>
    group_by(source, target) |>
    summarise(
        weight = n(),
        lr_pairs = paste(lr_pair, collapse = ";"),
        .groups = "drop"
    )

head(ccc_edges)
```

## Storing pseudobulk data and CCC networks in a `GraphExperiment` object

Next, we will aggregate counts by cell type to obtain pseudobulk profiles,
so that observations (columns) are cell types. Then, we will create the
CCC graph, including all cell types as nodes, and add the
total number of outgoing and incoming interactions (i.e., the weighted
out- and in-degrees) as node attributes, which indicate
the roles of cell types as senders and receivers, respectively.

```{r}
# Create pseudobulk profiles
pb <- aggregateAcrossCells(
    sce, ids = sce$label, statistics = "sum", use.assay.type = "counts"
)
sizeFactors(pb) <- NULL # remove cell-level size factors
pb <- logNormCounts(pb)

pb

# Create CCC graph with all cell types as nodes
ccc_graph <- graph_from_data_frame(
    ccc_edges, directed = TRUE, vertices = data.frame(name = colnames(pb))
)
V(ccc_graph)$out_strength <- strength(ccc_graph, mode = "out")
V(ccc_graph)$in_strength <- strength(ccc_graph, mode = "in")

# Create `GraphExperiment` object
ge <- as(pb, "GraphExperiment")
colGraph(ge, "ccc") <- ccc_graph

ge
```

Node attributes are available in `colData`, along with
cell type metadata (e.g., number of cells per cell type).

```{r}
colData(ge) |>
    as.data.frame() |>
    select(ncells, ccc__out_strength, ccc__in_strength) |>
    arrange(-ccc__out_strength)
```

## Exploring the CCC network

Let's visualize the CCC network, with edge widths proportional to the number
of interactions, and node sizes proportional to the number of
outgoing interactions.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-dpi: 300

g <- colGraph(ge, "ccc")

ggraph(g, layout = "circle") +
    geom_edge_fan(
        aes(width = weight, alpha = weight),
        arrow = arrow(length = unit(2.5, "mm"), type = "closed"),
        end_cap = circle(6, "mm"), color = "steelblue"
    ) +
    geom_edge_loop(aes(width = weight, alpha = weight), color = "steelblue") +
    geom_node_point(aes(size = out_strength), color = "firebrick") +
    geom_node_text(aes(label = name), repel = TRUE, size = 4) +
    scale_edge_width(range = c(0.3, 2.5)) +
    scale_edge_alpha(range = c(0.3, 0.9), guide = "none") +
    scale_size_continuous(range = c(2, 10)) +
    theme_graph(base_family = "sans") +
    labs(edge_width = "Number of\ninteractions", size = "Outgoing\ninteractions")
```

Since ligand-receptor pairs are stored as edge attributes, we can easily
explore which interactions underlie each edge. For instance, let's see the
ligand-receptor pairs between activated stellate cells (the main senders)
and endothelial cells.

```{r}
# Get ligand-receptor pairs for a particular edge
e <- E(g)[.from("activated_stellate") & .to("endothelial")]
lr_pairs <- strsplit(e$lr_pairs, ";")[[1]]
length(lr_pairs)
head(lr_pairs, 15)
```

Graph algorithms can also be used to explore the network. For instance,
we can use PageRank to identify the most important receivers of signals,
and then check the expression of the receptors involved in the pseudobulk
profiles, which are stored in the same object.

```{r}
# PageRank centrality (receivers of many signals from important senders)
sort(page_rank(g, weights = E(g)$weight)$vector, decreasing = TRUE)

# Expression of receptors targeted by activated stellate cells
receptors <- liana_agg |>
    filter(aggregate_rank < 0.01, source == "activated_stellate") |>
    pull(receptor.complex) |>
    strsplit("_") |>
    unlist() |>
    unique()

round(logcounts(ge)[intersect(receptors, rownames(ge)), ], 1) |> head(10)
```
